It seems to me that galleries function in that way, where that type of expression is given a platform, but then to take that outside the gallery and just place it in a public context, suddenly that artistic expression becomes slightly unpalatable in a way. Which is what public art was always not about, it was about not directly taking art objects and introducing them into public spaces...I guess the more recent tradition of public art was about criticising that.

Well that is something that needs to be explained to people because if you leave it to people it doesn't look like art. You see, when you see bulbs you immediately think of carnival, you don't think of art.

Most people ask 'what are the lights for?' People don't know. Because there is no sign or anything to say this is from Camden Arts Centre. People don't know why. They keep asking me everyday. 'What are the lights for?'

I think you've got to be careful because, for example, I think that Gormley thing up near Newcastle is really offensive. Really, really appalling. I think it's terrible that people have to have that inflicted upon them. It's so ugly and what it stands for is really offensive. Is it some sort of Christian thing or something? I think some of it's great. But it's really tricky. But something which everyone can appreciate is fine. I wouldn't say, 'oh yes lets have lots of public art so we can challenge people's conceptions'.... by having, I don't know, lots of menstruating cows, something really stupid. I mean, I know lots of people who do art and some of them can be really offensive in a really tedious way. Shock value, in inverted commas.

This is nice, it's decorative. Let's have things which look beautiful and are aesthetic. I mean I'm an aesthetician actually. I'm just finishing a book on beauty now, in the next few days. Let's have things which are nice to look at....ok here's something...for things in a gallery let's have things which are heavy on meaning but in public spaces, maybe you need things which just look great, beautiful, pretty or enhancing. I think it is difficult because you have to have art which appeals to everyone. And if you just have things for Guardian readers...There's no reason why you should be spending money on people who have got money anyway. I've got quite simple tastes. I like things which are pretty. I get bored analysing art.

I certainly think artists should have a sense of responsibility. That's a pretty unusual thing to do. Look at it now. If you talk to journalists, they say 'What does it matter as long as I can sell my papers?' There is no responsibility in business and journalism and I think the British art world now is so driven by media attention. I think people should be aware of their responsibilities, much more in public art that in private spaces.

Peter was quite keen that the work was shown in a library context rather than a gallery because it was about being in the community. With this a library space almost became like an exhibition space, it became like a little cinema in some ways, it's a really nice bridge area. And the way that we set up the screens on the glass it became a sort of intermediary space and I found that quite exciting particularly because we've got...I'm in another meeting now where we're talking because we've got a six and a half million refurbishment coming up starting in the new year and so, I don't know whether this would happen, but part of what I wanted was a more flexible use of the building that we could blur the boundaries a bit between arts and libraries and also the sports centre, because we're linking in with the sports centre. And that seemed to work really well in that project, it felt like a number of people were coming together and also dealing with different communities.

I found it interesting in terms of the art that was made. In terms of, how do you read it? The whole thing about the boundary of art, when does it become gallery art, when does it become community art, or is there any difference? 'Journeys' was an art level of presentation, a gallery kind of presentation, but at the same time you were working with people in the community who aren't necessarily trained in a fine art discipline. I found it surprising how well that worked. And I would have thought that that was one of the big successes of the piece. Because people could come in along the level of 'oh that's my brother who's telling this story, and that's our house', something like that, but at the same time, the way that....because there were headphones as well so you could listen, and if you were deaf and you could sign, you could read it easier than if you were hearing which was a nice contrast. Then, the signing wasn't always in sync with what the images were, and I just enjoyed that. The co-ordination of it, or the choreography of it.

I think we could have done better in getting more people in to see the work. I don't think a huge number of people came. And it might have been to nice to have done more work in terms of getting people in, I don't know, maybe having events on days beyond the opening. I don't think we had any artists' talks.
Very good. Interesting. I learnt lots.

Brilliant informations - aim for hearing people about deaf issues and deaf cultures.
The video was wonderful but the exhibition was poorly advertised and sign-posted. You need more posters in the entrance here and elsewhere.
A wonderful opportunity and method of communication through the arts. Very entertaining.
Well worth a trip to London for. Sensitive, informed and informative. Hopefully the first of more work of this nature.

Was it his idea? So it wasn't evoked by Camden Council? That was my initial reaction, which was, I suppose, the surprise that somebody, somewhere in this huge organisation has actually said 'this is a mess, it's not pleasant, it's not conducive to a relaxed atmosphere', somebody's come along and they've tidied it up, this can't be right! So in fact it wasn't Camden Council at all? They had nothing to do with it? I mean if it was intended to be a piece of art, I didn't get the art...I didn't see any promotional material for it. Was there? Yeah, but three quarters of what comes through is junk mail. Oh, I've seen that leaflet. I didn't look at it. Because it's not what we do, we're busy people. It's a shame they took the gravel away, that's all. It was very nice. I don't hold an opinion...in fact I'm quite glad that Camden Council didn't do it though. I would have said it was a waste of money and I would have been very angry.

The leaflet is very official looking. It's very government looking. It's the sort of thing you would do that to (tosses it to one side). You need to build up a community spirit, don't you, in an area, to understand where it's going and where it's come from. Well I don't know who else really does, other than artists, that's the thing. Otherwise it's just a place where there are public systems and people live there. Although you do get those little plaques...'somebody famous lived here'. But this is something more now, something that's current.

I can see what Maurice is doing will attract lots of attention but what is it actually going to set out to achieve ultimately? What is the actual end goal, that's what I can't see at the moment. And the actual value at the end of the day, is it an artistic value, or is it just raising awareness in the local community, in local business? I'm not sure about that one.

Once an artist is commissioned for something, his art is on a business footing. You're accountable to whoever has contracted you. But I think there's always going to be a conflict because artists have to be paid for their work, otherwise you wouldn't live and I wonder...was this initiated by Camden Arts or by London Borough of Camden? The Council don't have any say? Oh that's good.

I think you can do without art but the world would be a cold and boring place, you do need art to stretch you. I feel any large development or whatever should benefit the local community. You're feeding off people...you're giving them something as well...it's reciprocal. There's a benefit to having art in there somewhere, providing it doesn't have a detrimental effect, not perhaps too radical or whatever, no Damien Hirst stuff. And obviously as we've got a multi-cultural society, especially in Camden. Lots of different races, ideals, beliefs and manners. I think it has to be pretty soft art really perhaps rather than 'in your face'.

Artists have obviously a natural ability as well as a trained eye to appreciate things in a certain light, to look at things in a particular way which normal people, the planners, the architects, whatever, don't see. Whereas an artist, the creative part...it's what is in there, the mind, how that works. So I think they can bring a lot more to a community or society anyway. As long as it's inoffensive. I think they can soften society, because society is basically a hard place.

I think we can all create art. Art isn't something for the elite. I think that English society is better than a lot of societies, but I think that most people don't get a chance to try their hand at it. So sadly most of us don't produce art but I think that we all have the potential.

Because there's a raw energy and a scrappiness to the making, you come in and you think it's a school class or kindergarten class. There is a kind of anti-aesthetic to it all. Which has got it's own strength, but there's a familiarity which is beyond the presentation of the works on the partitions. I was walking around thinking 'so what?' I thought it was an invitation to interact - and that's quite intimidating, and it's never made clear what to do if you're invited to interact anyway. The concept is actually more exciting than the actual show. The visuals produced...we've seen a lot of public art, collaboration works - and the visuals tend to suffer.

It's got a certain energy to it and it's got a life. But I would be more interested in the documentation of the making of it or into the patients own interpretation of their ideas. Rather that an artist taking that material and presenting it in a way which is supposed to suggest authorship.

I think that exhibitions like this rely on really strong interpretation. It's not that the concept is everything, but it plays a really big part in appreciation and understanding and education. I'm all for a bit of bumpf in galleries anyway, a bit of direct interpretation. There shouldn't be that distance between the art and the audience. You can definitely be brought a bit closer.
If you take it into something else, or allow them to do something with it, maybe that would have been interesting, I don't know. It's just become wallpaper. It misses a text.

I think to take away the authority of display and framing, actually works in this project. Because that museum way of seeing, is authoritative. So when the work was created, had the people seen this space, had they visited Camden Arts Centre, and were they aware of the agendas and the whole history?

The visual art world has become so elitist, that because people don't know about art history, it's hard for them to understand what art is about anyway and what they are looking for when they see something, so it's purely based on design, commercialism or popular culture. They don't know what's good or bad because they don't know what to look for. They'll be looking at a piece just like they look at MTV or a brand new car to buy.

We've been here for about two months. There's not really any community-type places around here, there's no markets. All I seem to end up doing is walking up and down the Finchley Road to the tube and back, with no interaction with anything around here, there are no market stalls or anything like that. I think the closest is Camden which I'm off to now.

Do they sincerely want to resolve issues or do they really want to invest in people? I don't know enough about the financial side. London is chaotic. The service sucks. Public transport's pretty good. But what really is terrible is the whole service industry, like you order something and something else arrives and then you ring up and no one knows what you're talking about, the whole town runs like that. You can't get what you want. It takes like, three times.

If you saw what it was like before, those walls and derelict shops there. The way they were covered in posters, they were dirty, the paint was peeling off, it was smelly because people used to use it to urinate against at night. It was such an eyesore that it was incredible to describe. Since they've done that I've spoken to people from across the road there, the optician, Shelfstore, and they're saying how lovely it is now. Before, it was terrible, it was like that for years and years and years, no one ever did anything about it.

I thought that somebody thought, 'let's get this cleaned up, why do we have to live in this...why does it have to be like this?' Because it really was horrible. It's been like that from time immemorial I'm afraid.

Oh, definitely the area is becoming more leisure oriented, yes. The O2 is all leisure, which is a big problem really. All the local retailers and shop owners had assumed, prior to it just being leisure, that in fact, it was going to be retail or a mix of things. Because there's no retail in there, its lost it's life. At night it takes off.

There are humans round here. Somewhere. There isn't a community. There isn't. I mean people do live here, they're upstairs and across the road but there is no community spirit, none at all. No there isn't anything here at all. I mean he's absolutely right, they are all commercial messages out there, or public messages. There's nothing for those driving through to think 'people live here, humans are here somewhere', there's nothing like that at all, is there? Even though there are. I mean a lot of it's bedsit land but it shouldn't detract from it, in fact it should be lively because of it. There's a lot of residents behind us. You wouldn't know it. It's a typical thing, you don't know your neighbour in London. You just don't do you? You get on with it.

Maybe there isn't so much of a sense of community in this area. Maybe in some areas there are more...but London's a big city, so as such you won't find good neighbourhoods on a high scale, it's difficult, because people are so busy. We live in a technology generation now, people will spend ten hours on a computer but they wouldn't spend ten minutes talking to an old neighbour, let's generalise a bit, I'm talking about 90%. So they are talking to the whole world, but they are not talking to their neighbour. There is a big paradox happening, very strong. But that will have to change, because the computer is here for us to use it, not for it to manipulate us. And that's getting very fast because six months from now, everything's obsolete. If you don't have your own individual identification in a more philosophical way, you go with the flow and you just lose it because you think for you to be up-to-date you have to follow the technology. And you put that as a very important thing, a priority, then you are trapped. Technology is very much available...yes, so that affects our neighbourhood.

I think we are living in a time where...I don't know, the reasons could be several.... basically it's a lack of...a very good friend of mine says 'we have so much comfort these days but we have less peace.' Individual peace. If you go around at six o'clock in the rush hour, you see madness. What for? What's the hurry? What cannot be done in ten minutes that has to be done in one minute? Is that nine minutes off your life, aghh...you know. You ask, 'it can't be so urgent that everyone else is doing it.' Ok, if thirty percent of people do it, even fifty, but ninety percent! Something's going on in the whole society as if it was like the world was going to end. It's not! It's a creation. Maybe then that's why you have many technology, many materialism. Is everybody blind? So at the end you look back and how many friends do you have?

The people who come here do know each other well. Because the thing with Bingo players, once they get used to a certain club you find that 85% of them, they normally stick to the same club.

Why do you think people come to Bingo? One reason, to win money. I think the social thing comes after because if I come in here and I never win, I would stop coming. I have won plenty of times, but not here, in other places. But if I didn't win it I would stop.

It makes me crazy...oh the adverts, oh my God. And then what they charge for the license for the television now. It's unbelievable isn't it, it's over a hundred pounds. There's a little old Irish lady who comes here, she comes every night, she does. The youngsters, they only come now and again.

I swim every day in the pond. Whatever the weather. All year.
I walk there twice a week, very early in the morning. I just do it because I'm very early in the morning and I just can't think where else to go.

I go depending which way the wind's blowing. Well my theory is, if the wind's blowing this way then it blows the fumes into the roads over here. I go everyday and I know it well. I like the variety and the wildness of it, I guess.

I walk twice a day. I have a fairly normal walk. It depends how much time I'm allowing. Yes, about half past eight the first time...either then or at lunchtime and then at four or five o'clock depending on work.
I use the Heath so much. The Heath has been so many years in my life, I've been walking it for twenty-five years.
The viewing point with a quote from Wordsworth on it. It's the best bit of the Heath. Well, it is in the morning anyway because you can see the whole of London. It's just there.

I live just down in Kentish Town so I come up here quite a bit. And I usually try and go for a bike ride on the Heath really early, when it's a bit earlier because not too many people are around. Just around there and you're not really supposed to cycle there, so...but if you go early enough, before the dog walkers start...

There is a strong refugee, maybe second, third generation community, Jewish community living round there and my immediate reference would be them, who came over in the 30s and 40s and moved into that area and I don't know whether....it was a very dramatic title somehow. The first person I went swimming in that pond with, she probably wouldn't describe herself as a refugee but she is essentially a refugee from Eastern Europe, and I think that would probably be the case for quite a number of a certain generation who use that pond.

Another thing about the ponds is that element of trust. There's no lockers, you don't pay to go in. You just hang up your kit and you go for a swim. And that's really extraordinary for London, isn't it?

Because what I found when I went to the pond...that's how I really got to know it, was going there every day and seeing it change, the weather changing and different groups coming and going and you get to know people as well, because there are some people who go every week, some people who go every day and they recognise you and they start to talk to you....And the idea of that being a community...it's not just Highgate, it is people from all over London that go there. Like for example the Men's Pond, you get boxers from the East End who use that regularly...or you get people who come from south London going up there once a week or something so, yes...

The idea for a carnival is good. People get together. Good atmosphere. It's good for the morale of the people. For people to get together. I think it somehow makes people feel good, forget different problems.

Oh yes. Community. You know neighbours. And I'll be quite honest you don't mix with everybody. 'Good morning.' 'Good afternoon.' But wherever you live you have to make the best of it. It doesn't mean that you have to mix with everybody but life is too short. If you live in a community you have to give and take.

On the right hand side you have got all these posh houses and the cricket club and a posh tennis club there. My foreign friends just say, 'well this is England', and it takes three months. I mean its comic. It should take a weekend.

And we're living in this grimy world of just day to day and getting things done and it's nice, because things are just utilitarian the whole time and you need something to cheer you up a bit. A lot of architecture, the exciting pieces, the swanky museums - a lot of buildings which aren't at the forefront of the architectural world, are very utilitarian, they just tend to make them grey or brown or something. If you went to a Mediterranean country, they'd paint them a bright colour, they'd take more care of it. I think things which enhance the environment are very important. So I'm quite positive.

It's like from home to America. From America to home. It's lovely. You could be there and thinking of here. It's funny that people in America might read it and it's got directions to Sainsburys.

I don't know. All I'll say is that the first time I stood out there and read that sign, a little tear came to the corner of my eye and I thought, 'that's absolutely fantastic that someone has done that.
